newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Rio +5 environment meeting raises few expectations.
newsitem.headline: Rio +5 environment meeting raises few expectations.

text.p: Five years after the Earth Summit another international gathering is opening in Rio de Janeiro on Thursday to review the pledges made in 1992, but environmentalists expect few tangible achievements from the Rio +5 Forum.

The conference at Rio's Sheraton Hotel is bringing together some 500 business leaders, representatives from citizen groups, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and United Nations agencies to find ways of implementing the goals set out in 1992.
Former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev, World Bank President James Wolfensohn and Director General of the World Trade Organisation Renato Ruggiero are expected to address the March 13-19 meeting.
Unlike the Earth Summit no heads of state or government representatives will be attending.

"This conference does not have the power to approve conventions and declarations. It raises fewer expectations," World Wildlife Fund spokesman Paulo Lyra said. "But it is an important conference because it will help to make governments fulfil their commitments."
Lyra said the conference would give NGOs and citizens an opportunity to better assess what governments and societies had actually done toward implementing the Earth Summit agenda.
"This conference is an instance of debt collection," Greenpeace campaign co-ordinator Delcio Rodrigues said. "There is a long line of countries which have not fulfilled their pledges."
Rio de Janeiro itself, as the host city of both environmental meetings, has failed to stand out as a shining example of evironmental correctness.

Pledges made in conjunction with the staging of the Earth Summit to clean up Guanabara Bay on which Rio stands have not been fulfilled to date due to political wrangling, despite a $350-million loan from the Inter-American Development Bank.
Failure to do so recently cost the city the chance to host the 2004 Olympic Games.

Like many other countries, Brazil still has to implement its pledges on reducing "greenhouse gases," believed to cause global warming, and a national commission for sustainable development has yet to meet.

The organisers of Rio +5 hope the conference will come up with a series of recommendations and strategies to be presented at a United Nations meeting in New York in June that will show ways for governments to put into action their commitments.
"The conference is organised around workshops that produce action," said Maximo Kalaw, executive director of the Earth Council NGO, one of the driving forces behind the Earth Summit and Rio +5.
"We have to translate and integrate environmental requirements into economic and social policies."
